run.title: Lean validation
run.objective: Decide whether an idea has been tested for demand, or only assumed to have it.
explainer: Most products do not fail because the build was bad. They fail because nobody checked whether anyone wanted the thing before the building started. The assumption underneath the whole plan was never tested.

Lean validation is the discipline of answering one question first — is the demand actually there — as quickly and as cheaply as possible. The contrast is stark in cost. Building first and asking later takes six to eighteen months and lakhs of rupees before you learn anything. A validation test takes seven to fourteen days and can cost a few thousand rupees, sometimes nothing at all.

The trap is that building feels like progress and testing feels like delay. It is the other way round: the test is the cheap way to buy certainty, and the build is the expensive way to buy the same information later.

worked.setup: A founder plans a six-month build for an AI meeting recorder, then a marketing campaign to launch it.
worked.move: Before the build, run a landing page with a clear offer and see whether anyone acts.
worked.because: The campaign already assumes demand exists. Validation tests that assumption while it is still cheap to be wrong.

glossary.plain: Answering “does anyone want this” quickly and cheaply, before building.
Spending months building on an assumption nobody tested.
Evidence that real people will act — not that they say the idea sounds good.
A single page describing the offer, used to see whether people act on it.

run.title: Landing page validation
run.objective: Judge whether a conversion rate is trustworthy by looking at who produced it.
explainer: A validation landing page is not a marketing landing page. A marketing page tries to maximise signups. A validation page tries to produce an honest reading, which sometimes means a lower number.

The trap is the warm network. Friends, followers, and colleagues are already inclined to support you, so a 40% signup rate from that audience is not a market signal — it is a politeness signal. The same page shown to cold, targeted traffic that matches your intended customer might convert at 8%, and that 8% is the more trustworthy of the two numbers.
So a conversion rate is never read alone. It is read together with the traffic that produced it. A rate without its audience is not evidence.

worked.setup: Two pages both report an 8% signup rate. Page A was shown to targeted traffic matching the intended customer. Page B went to friends, employees, and a giveaway list.
worked.move: Treat Page A as the usable signal and discard Page B's rate.
worked.because: Identical percentages can carry completely different evidence, because the people behind them had different reasons to click.

glossary.plain: A page built to produce an honest demand reading, not the highest possible signup count.
The share of visitors who take the chosen action.
Friends, followers, and colleagues — an audience biased toward supporting you.
A result that looks like demand but was produced by the wrong audience or by chance.
The share of visitors who leave without engaging at all.

run.title: Pre-sales and commitment strength
run.objective: Rank demand evidence by what it cost the person to give it.
explainer: Pre-sales validation asks for a real commitment before anything is built. It exists because evidence is only as strong as the cost of producing it.

That produces a commitment spectrum. Praise in a survey costs nothing. A like costs nothing. Opening an email costs nothing. A signup costs a little attention. A letter of intent costs reputation. A payment — even a partial, refundable one — costs money, and money is the hardest commitment to fake.

This is why a person who clicks is curious, a person who signs up is interested, and a person who pays even a small deposit is behaving like an actual customer. When you need the highest confidence before committing to a build, you ask for the costliest signal you can reasonably request.

worked.setup: A team needs to decide whether to build. They have 200 survey positives, 30 wait-list signups, and 4 paid deposits.
worked.move: Treat the 4 deposits as the primary evidence and the 200 survey positives as background.
worked.because: The deposits are the only responses where someone gave up something real.

glossary.plain: Asking for a real commitment — usually payment — before building.
Ranking responses by what they cost the person: praise < click < signup < letter of intent < payment.
A written statement of intent to buy — costs reputation, not money.
Someone who might buy, being tested for how far they will actually go.

run.title: MVP validation logic
run.objective: Combine the module's tools into a single build-or-not decision under real constraints.
explainer: This is the integration lecture: everything from the previous five comes together into one decision framework.

An MVP — minimum viable product — is what you build when you do not have the time, money, or people for the full thing. It performs the basic job the real product is meant to do, for roughly ten to twenty percent of the effort. It is not a worse product; it is a smaller question.

The decision to build rests on stacked signals rather than any single one. Interest shown through behaviour on a landing page or smoke test is the first. A real commitment — at least one pre-sale, deposit, or letter of intent — is the second. A repeatable way to reach the same kind of customer again is the third. One signal alone is a hint. Together they are a reason to build.

worked.setup: A team has a working smoke test at 8% from targeted traffic, two paid deposits, and a channel that reliably reaches the same audience.
worked.move: Build the minimum viable version that does the core job, not the full roadmap.
worked.because: Three independent signals justify a small build; they do not yet justify a large one.

glossary.plain: Minimum viable product — the smallest build that does the core job, at 10-20% of the effort.
A planned test with a stated signal and a decision attached to the result.
An MVP that actually works, as opposed to a smoke test where nothing is built.

handoff.connects: Module 1 asked whether anyone wants it. Module 2 asks whether a measured difference is real.
